output.title: When opt-in records stop being trustworthy
output.body:
If opt-in records stop being trustworthy, treat that as a workflow check before the next send, not as a broad AI project. The question is simple: can you tell, for each contact, whether consent is current, withdrawn, stale, or unclear? If you cannot, do not guess.

For a small business owner, the failure usually shows up as manual checking, a spreadsheet full of edge cases, or the habit of sending because the list is there. That is where the time leak starts. In the approved persona scenario, repetitive manual work is already a real drag; messy consent records can add to it. Keep that number in its original lane, though: the 8–10 hours is a persona scenario for repeated customer questions, neglected leads, and manual invoice/data work, not a measured cost of consent review.

One practical next step is to mark every contact as current, stale, or unknown based on the evidence you already have, then route stale and unknown records away from the send list. That can be manual, spreadsheet-based, or automation-assisted depending on your tools. If your email system already keeps consent history or supports clean segmentation, use that as the first diagnostic. If it does not, a small workflow check in your own environment may be enough to expose the gap. Human approval still stays in the loop for any send decision. Better a boring list review than a polite mistake.
